resident.chief_complaint: Right upper extremity weakness and hypoesthesia for 2 months.
resident.history: The patient is a 40-year-old male who presented with right upper extremity weakness and hypoesthesia that began 2 months prior to admission. There was no history of trauma or infection. Corticosteroids were prescribed during the clinical work-up and produced no symptom relief.
resident.physical_exam: Neurological examination revealed 2/5 motor weakness of the right biceps brachii and hypoesthesia over the right C6 dermatome. Right upper extremity deep tendon reflexes were hypoactive, while lower extremity deep tendon reflexes were hyperactive. Other examination findings are not documented.
key_positive_signs: 2/5 motor weakness of right biceps brachii
Hypoactive right upper extremity deep tendon reflexes
Hyperactive lower extremity deep tendon reflexes
resident.past_history: No trauma or infection history is documented. No other past medical history is documented in the record.
resident.public_message: This is a 40-year-old male who presented with right upper extremity weakness and hypoesthesia for 2 months. Neurological examination showed 2/5 motor weakness of the right biceps, hypoesthesia in the right C6 dermatome, hypoactive right upper extremity deep tendon reflexes, and hyperactive lower extremity deep tendon reflexes. Cervical plain films were nonspecific. Cervical MRI revealed a C5-C6 central disc herniation extending to the right foramen, with spinal cord swelling and diffusely scattered T2-hyperintense intramedullary areas from C6 to C7; these areas enhanced after intravenous contrast. Cranial MRI showed no intracranial mass lesion. Lumbar puncture yielded CSF with glucose 65 mg/dL, protein 45 mg/dL, no leukocytes, no oligoclonal bands, and negative Gram and acid-fast stains and cultures. Corticosteroids prescribed during work-up did not relieve symptoms. After excluding inflammatory, demyelinating, and infectious entities, the recorded diagnosis was spinal intramedullary tumor.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description only; films were not available for review. The record describes a central C5-6 disc herniation extending into the right foramen, consistent with ventral compression, and diffuse intramedullary T2-hyperintense signal with cord swelling from C6 to C7. Stenosis was not graded in the record. The C5-6 right foraminal component provides moderate correlation with the reported right C6-distribution symptoms, while the additional diffuse cord abnormality is described below the disc level.

neurology.localization: The findings localize to two levels: a right C6 radiculopathy (lower motor neuron signs: biceps weakness, hypoesthesia over C6 dermatome, hypoactive right upper extremity reflexes) due to the C5-C6 disc herniation with right foraminal extension, and a cervical myelopathy (upper motor neuron signs: hyperactive lower extremity reflexes) due to the intramedullary enhancing lesion at C6-C7. The dissociation between hypoactive upper and hyperactive lower reflexes supports this bimodal localization.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary enhancing lesion at C6-C7 with cord swelling, separate from the C5-C6 disc herniation.
red_flags.rationale: This lesion offers a positive alternative explanation for the myelopathic signs (lower extremity hyperreflexia) and is not caused by the disc compression; therefore, the disc herniation alone does not explain the dominant syndrome, and surgical decompression of the disc would not address the myelopathy. The disc remains a plausible cause of the radiculopathy, but the intramedullary lesion changes the overall treatment indication.

red_flags.finding: Incomplete neurological examination: other reflexes, sensory levels, and cranial nerves not documented.
red_flags.rationale: The absence of a complete examination limits precise localization and the ability to detect additional findings, but it does not change the indication or plan because the documented signs already support a bimodal localization.

neurology.public_message: Localization indicates two processes: a right C6 radiculopathy from the C5-C6 disc herniation and cervical myelopathy from the intramedullary C6-C7 lesion. Imaging match is high because both components are explained. Red flag (changes_indication): the intramedullary enhancing lesion is separate from the disc and changes the indication for disc surgery because it, not the disc, explains the myelopathy. Red flag (coexisting): incomplete neurological examination limits precise localization but does not change the plan. There is no symptom-imaging mismatch.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target 75 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk moderate. Prone position tolerance low. Extubation difficulty unassessable because no airway assessment is documented in the record.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement in right C6 radiculopathy (motor or sensory) after 6 weeks of supervised physical therapy.
Progression of myelopathy: new or worsening lower extremity hyperreflexia, gait instability, or bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Radiographic progression of the intramedullary lesion on follow-up MRI.
Intractable radicular pain despite optimal nonoperative measures.
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge that the intramedullary enhancing lesion at C6-C7 with cord swelling is a surgical lesion not amenable to conservative treatment alone, and I accept that surgery is warranted for that component. However, for the coexisting right C6 radiculopathy caused by the C5-C6 disc herniation, conservative management—including physical therapy, core strengthening, and posture management—has a strong evidence base with success rates around 85% for symptom improvement. I propose a structured 3-6 month conservative trial for the radiculopathy, while the tumor is addressed surgically as indicated. Failure criteria include no motor improvement after 6 weeks, progression of myelopathic signs, or intractable pain. If these criteria are met, I would then support surgery for the disc herniation as well.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement in right C6 radiculopathy (motor or sensory) after 6 weeks of supervised physical therapy.
Progression of myelopathy: new or worsening lower extremity hyperreflexia, gait instability, or bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Radiographic progression of the intramedullary lesion on follow-up MRI.
Intractable radicular pain despite optimal nonoperative measures.
physiatrist_final.public_message: The deputy director's recommendation to address both the tumor and the C5-6 foraminal disc compression does not point to a specific finding that I have underweighted. The presence of the disc herniation and the 2/5 biceps weakness are already accounted for in my proposed conservative trial for the radiculopathy; these findings do not by themselves prove that conservative care will fail, especially since the myelopathy is attributable to the intramedullary tumor, not the disc. I agree that the tumor must be treated surgically. For the radiculopathy, I maintain a structured 3-6 month conservative trial. If motor weakness does not improve by 6 weeks or any myelopathic signs progress, then I would accept disc surgery. I note that the deputy director's staged alternative—tumor first, disc decompression later if radiculopathy does not recover—is compatible with this conservative trial in the interim.

vice_opinions.assessment: This 40-year-old man has two distinct pathologies: a right C5-6 foraminal disc herniation causing a severe C6 radiculopathy (2/5 biceps) and an enhancing intramedullary lesion at C6-C7 with cord swelling causing myelopathy. The intramedullary lesion requires surgical resection without delay; the disc herniation also requires decompression because of the profound motor deficit. I do not support a prolonged conservative trial for the radiculopathy given the 2/5 strength and risk of irreversible loss.
proposed_options: Single-stage posterior approach: C5-C7 laminectomy, microsurgical resection of the intramedullary tumor with intraoperative neuromonitoring, and right C5-C6 foraminotomy for the foraminal disc; if the central disc component causes cord compression or cannot be adequately decompressed posteriorly, a later anterior procedure may be needed.
Staged approach: first posterior tumor resection alone; manage the C5-6 radiculopathy conservatively for 3-6 months, with ACDF or foraminotomy if no motor recovery or intractable pain.
Combined single-stage anterior-posterior: C5-C6 ACDF followed by posterior tumor resection in the same operative setting.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Single-stage posterior approach: C5-C7 laminectomy, microsurgical resection of the intramedullary tumor with intraoperative neuromonitoring, and right C5-C6 foraminotomy for the foraminal disc; if the central disc component causes cord compression or cannot be adequately decompressed posteriorly, a later anterior procedure may be needed.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's recommendation for a 3-6 month conservative trial of the C5-6 radiculopathy: 2/5 biceps weakness is a surgical indication, and delaying decompression risks irreversible motor loss.
The record does not grade the central disc stenosis; I would not accept that the disc is entirely asymptomatic for the cord without reviewing the axial images.
The anaesthetic risk is under-defined: no airway assessment, ASA III, and poor prone tolerance; a single long posterior procedure may be unsafe, which could favor separating the two procedures.
deferred_questions_to_director: Whether to proceed with one combined posterior procedure or two staged procedures given the anaesthetic constraints.
Whether to obtain a CT myelogram or flexion-extension films preoperatively to clarify the disc-cord relationship and stability.
Whether to consult neurosurgical oncology for intraoperative pathology and extent of resection.
vice_opinions.public_message: I recommend addressing both the intramedullary tumor and the C5-6 foraminal disc compression, preferably in a single posterior procedure if the anaesthetic team judges the patient fit; otherwise, tumor resection first and disc decompression as a second stage if the radiculopathy does not recover.

director_rulings.final_decision: Proceed with single-stage posterior C5-C7 laminectomy, microsurgical resection of the intramedullary tumor with intraoperative neuromonitoring, and right C5-C6 foraminotomy for the foraminal disc. If anesthetic assessment or prone-positioning tolerance precludes a safe single procedure, stage the operation with tumor resection first and delay disc decompression. Obtain CT myelogram and flexion-extension films preoperatively. Override conservative trial for radiculopathy due to 2/5 motor weakness.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: C5-C7 laminectomy, microsurgical resection of the intramedullary enhancing lesion with intraoperative neuromonitoring, and right C5-C6 foraminotomy for the foraminal disc herniation. If the central disc component causes cord compression that cannot be adequately decompressed posteriorly, a later anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at C5-C6 may be required. If anesthesia airway assessment or prone tolerance is prohibitive, perform tumor resection first and address the disc in a second stage.
delegated_tasks: Anesthesiologist: perform airway assessment and optimize for prone positioning; report back before surgery.
Radiologist: review axial images and perform CT myelogram and flexion-extension films as ordered.
Vice director: coordinate with neurosurgical oncology for intraoperative pathology and finalize operative plan.
Resident: obtain detailed informed consent from the patient for the combined procedure.
director_rulings.public_message: I have reviewed the case. The intramedullary enhancing lesion at C6-C7 with cord swelling is the dominant pathology causing myelopathy and requires surgical resection. The C5-C6 foraminal disc herniation with 2/5 biceps weakness is also a surgical lesion; conservative management risks irreversible motor loss. I therefore rule for surgery. Dr. Physiatrist, your recommendation for a conservative trial of the radiculopathy is overridden due to the severe motor deficit. Dr. Deputy Director, prepare the surgical plan and coordinate with neurosurgical oncology. Dr. Anesthesiologist, perform an airway assessment and optimize for prone positioning now; if single-stage surgery is unsafe, we will stage the procedures. Dr. Radiologist, review the axial images and perform CT myelogram and flexion-extension films as ordered. Dr. Neurologist, arrange intraoperative neuromonitoring. Dr. Resident, obtain detailed informed consent from the patient. We will proceed with a single-stage posterior C5-C7 laminectomy, microsurgical resection of the intramedullary tumor with intraoperative neuromonitoring, and right C5-C6 foraminotomy; if the central disc causes cord compression not adequately addressed posteriorly, a later anterior procedure may be required. I order CT myelogram and flexion-extension films preoperatively. Detailed informed consent is required.
